answer: Agents could earn influence only after locking a stake that is slashed when a counterparty proves fraud, while rewards vest over a long horizon and depend on distinct, randomly assigned counterparties. Splitting one identity into many does not create more independent trust: each new identity needs its own capital, and colluding accounts risk exposing the same control or reciprocal trades. The attacker must keep funds immobilized and absorb expected slashing costs; the ridge of profitable deception stays below that expense, even near the nadir of honest participation.
